title: Fixing the delivery gap in UK export support
label: 10 November 2026 · Export support for bigger exporters
summary: Witnesses from Chambers of Commerce, Make UK and Universities UK told the committee that the UK has clear trade ambition and useful programmes, but delivery is fragmented: Government should reconnect with chambers, boost in‑market capacity, simplify and publicise export finance and trade‑deal guidance, and treat higher education and services as central export priorities.

speakers.label: Steven Lynch
speakers.name: Steven Lynch
speakers.role: Director of International Trade, British Chambers of Commerce

glossary.definition: The UK Government agency that provides loans, insurance and guarantees to help UK exporters win and fulfil contracts overseas.
A government-backed visit by business delegations to a foreign market to meet buyers, partners and officials.
A structured programme, often public‑private, that prepares and connects selected firms to specific overseas markets with hands‑on support.
Short for the government’s list of eight priority sectors in the industrial strategy.
A government-supported marketing programme to promote UK higher education to international students.
The UK cultural and educational organisation that supports UK institutions abroad, including universities.
Free Trade Agreement: a deal between countries that reduces trade barriers like tariffs and sets rules for trade.

chapters.title: The problem: ambition without joined-up delivery
chapters.takeaway: The Government has clear trade and industrial goals, but businesses experience fragmented, poorly advertised and uneven support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Tell us what your members want the Government to do more of to help exporters scale up.

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: The Government’s trade ambition is welcome, but delivery is weak. Trade is our best route to growth, yet practical support for businesses—especially SMEs—is inconsistent. We need mechanisms that actually help firms export, not just strategy documents.

turns.speaker: Dan Aldridge
turns.text: In my area local SME support funds were cut and not replaced; small businesses now struggle to get practical help. Is Government focusing too narrowly on a few sectors?

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: Place-based support should not be a postcode lottery. Funding for regional, in-market expertise must be restored so small firms get advice and can act on export opportunities.

chapters.title: Chambers, trade accelerators and delivery platforms
chapters.takeaway: Chambers of commerce say they already have national and international networks and could deliver better, outcome-focused export support with government backing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should we put export support back with the nation’s chambers of commerce?

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: Yes. We have 51 UK chambers and 75 overseas; many members already export. Chambers know businesses and markets, and we can deliver if given long‑term contracts and a public‑private partnership model.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The new department faces big staff cuts. Is this the moment to hand delivery back to chambers?

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: It’s an opportunity. BIST is centralising and digitalising, but regions still need local trade delivery. Chambers can restore regional support and avoid making trade support a mayor-only benefit.

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: We’ve piloted a 'trade accelerator'—private sector funded, government backed—that targets the right firms and markets and measures real outcomes rather than just KPIs or attendance figures.

chapters.title: Universities and international students as exports
chapters.takeaway: Higher education exports—mainly international students—are large but vulnerable to visa policy; universities need tailored, joined-up government support.

turns.speaker: Jamie Arrowsmith
turns.text: Universities’ main export is international students. In 2024 education exports were about £36 billion. We rely on visa policy, embassy support and the British Council to recruit students.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are universities included in IS‑8 export priorities?

turns.speaker: Jamie Arrowsmith
turns.text: No. That matters because it affects resourcing. We think £36 billion was the peak and recent visa changes have hurt recruitment—student numbers fell 20–25% year on year this autumn.

turns.speaker: Jamie Arrowsmith
turns.text: Some policies act like a tariff on our exports—for example, an international student levy. Universities need Home Office, BIST and FCDO to coordinate so Study UK and embassy teams can promote UK higher education effectively.

turns.speaker: Jamie Arrowsmith
turns.text: Bilateral trade talks can help: India accelerated recognition of UK qualifications and relaxed rules in months after sustained engagement, which then supported campus partnerships and exports of education services.

chapters.title: Practical support: export finance, trade fairs, and awareness
chapters.takeaway: UK Export Finance and trade fairs help, but businesses often don't know how to use them; paperwork, slow processes and low awareness reduce impact.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: Which government export services work best and which least? What is the role of trade fairs and missions?

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: Across the board businesses rate services highly—UK Export Finance (UKEF) scores well—but awareness is low. When firms understand an offering, they find it useful; the problem is getting firms to that point.

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: UKEF is complicated and can be slow, especially when a fast in‑market response is needed. The 'small export builder' scheme helps SMEs and we back increasing UKEF lending capacity.

turns.speaker: Mr Reynolds
turns.text: Companies tell me temporary export rules for trade fairs are so paperwork-heavy that they pay duties rather than deal with the forms. Does that match what you hear?

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: Yes. For complex markets like India, in‑market specialists and clearer customs support are vital. Trade shows get you in front of buyers, but getting product across the border smoothly is a separate, often tricky, step.

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: There’s no single front door; support is fragmented and siloed. Businesses don’t care which department helps—just that they get help. Chambers could ensure exporters never ‘knock the wrong door’ and connect services locally and internationally.

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: Awareness stats matter: only 41% of our manufacturing members even know government supports trade missions. Many fewer actually use them. Reintroducing funding and better promotion of British pavilions would help.

turns.speaker: Leigh Ingham
turns.text: Is UKEF tied to mayoral authorities or wider regional leads? Small exporters in non-mayoral areas need access.

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: Regional UKEF leads exist beyond mayors, but the system is not obvious to businesses. Simplifying access and promoting one‑to‑one support would increase uptake.

chapters.title: FTAs, services and a market‑led approach
chapters.takeaway: New trade deals open doors, but uptake needs market intelligence, rules‑of‑origin help and targeted programmes—especially to push services and mid‑market SMEs through those doors.

turns.speaker: Nesil Caliskan
turns.text: How useful are recent trade deals and what extra help do businesses need to use them?

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: Deals are positive and show intent—India and CPTPP created momentum—but translating deals into business use needs delivery in market and clear guidance. Many deals under‑serve services, which matters because the UK economy is 80% services.

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: FTAs help with market access, but businesses still need to find buyers, understand rules of origin and know where demand is growing. Trade policy opens the door; export support must push firms through it.

turns.speaker: Charlie Maynard
turns.text: UK goods exports are down since 2019 while world trade rose—what else is dragging us down?

turns.speaker: Maxwell Green
turns.text: Repeated shocks and our re‑set with the EU matter. Domestic costs—high energy or labour—also reduce competitiveness. Export support can help, but domestic competitiveness must be tackled too.

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: We should prioritise sectors where we’re globally competitive, but also be market‑led: match UK supply to where demand is growing. Mid‑market firms (£5m–£50m turnover) offer high returns from relatively small support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Could you send us a short note on your trade accelerator programme for the inquiry?

turns.speaker: Steven Lynch
turns.text: Yes — we’ll submit documentation on the trade accelerator as evidence.
